title: Context Recall Cards
user: Independent language learners who know a word in an app but cannot retrieve it in a real sentence; they need short, personally meaningful recall practice with pronunciation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker says learners do the usual streaks and flashcards for months yet still forget vocabulary when they need it, and asks which features make words stick.
A spaced-repetition user requests per-side audio recording/playback specifically to make pronunciation practice possible from their own cards.

recurrence: Two independent 2025–2026 learner-tool requests: vocabulary retention and personal pronunciation practice remain unsolved by generic card queues.
current_workaround: Make conventional Anki cards, save separate voice notes, or rely on app streaks and passive exposure.
incumbents_and_gap: Anki, AnkiDroid, and Duolingo schedule recall but do not make a learner's own sentence, voice attempt, and later production prompt one compact practice loop.
smallest_useful_product: Offline-first PWA for creating a word card from a learner-written sentence and optional recording; it schedules listen, cloze, and speak-back prompts and shows the original context. Non-goals: AI-generated mnemonics, a language course, social feeds, or speech scoring claims.
success_measure: In a four-week pilot, 50% of learners add 30+ personal contexts and complete a delayed spoken recall for at least 70% of them.
monetization: one-time — personal recordings and durable offline ownership make a straightforward paid utility more credible than a retention subscription.
constraints: Keep recordings on device by default; consent before sharing; use browser media APIs; no language-model or copyrighted-course dependency.
why_distinct: The unit is a learner-authored context-to-production loop, not a generated flashcard deck or chat tutor.

title: Recall Calibrator
user: Spaced-repetition users who distrust their own Good/Hard/Easy judgment and want to know whether they can actually retrieve an answer.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A flashcard user directly asks why the app makes them self-rate instead of knowing how well they are memorizing.
The actively updated Anki thread proposing FSRS as the default has 68 reactions, showing sustained demand for better scheduling rather than manual habit alone.

recurrence: One direct learner complaint plus a 68-reaction scheduler discussion; erroneous self-assessment compounds across every review session.
current_workaround: Tap a subjective rating, use a strict personal rule, or change Anki scheduler settings without feedback about calibration.
incumbents_and_gap: Anki FSRS improves intervals from grades it receives; SuperMemo-style systems still largely require a grade. They do not show a learner whether their grading is systematically too generous or too harsh.
smallest_useful_product: A local review companion that samples typed exact/keyword recall before revealing an answer, compares it to the learner's grade, and reports personal calibration with exportable intervals. Non-goals: replacing Anki, automatic grading of essays, or an LLM tutor.
success_measure: After 200 sampled reviews, at least 60% of pilot users reduce the gap between self-grade and typed-recall result by 20% or more.
monetization: free — trustworthy calibration benefits from transparent local logic; paid import/export support can follow only if demanded.
constraints: Use deterministic matching and configurable accepted answers; keep answer text local; clearly label the result as a recall proxy, not a learning diagnosis.
why_distinct: It measures the reliability of the review signal feeding an SRS rather than competing on another scheduling algorithm.

title: Knowledge Note Bridge
user: Working self-learners who capture technical and business-domain knowledge in Markdown but need card updates without destroying existing review history.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker describes the dual problem of retaining technical concepts and domain knowledge, and asks how people capture both together long-term.
A user reports that editing their Markdown notes fails to update the current Anki deck, forcing new decks and losing review progress.

recurrence: Two independent 2025 requests expose the same friction: notes and long-lived practice records drift apart, making useful knowledge expensive to maintain.
current_workaround: Manually edit Anki, regenerate decks and lose history, or keep duplicate source material in notes and cards.
incumbents_and_gap: Obsidian plugins and AnkiConnect can generate cards, but their failures are hard to inspect and identity changes can silently reset a card's history.
smallest_useful_product: A local Markdown-to-Anki bridge with stable card IDs, a dry-run diff, explicit archive/rename handling, and a reversible history-preservation report. Non-goals: a note-taking app, cloud sync service, or automatic card generation.
success_measure: At least 90% of changed cards in pilot repositories retain the intended review history, with every destructive change previewed before sync.
monetization: one-time — this is episodic-but-high-stakes local workflow infrastructure rather than hosted content.
constraints: Back up collections before writes; use the documented Anki API or an export/import adapter; never transmit notes or decks by default.
why_distinct: It is an integrity layer for learner-owned source notes and review history, not another Markdown flashcard syntax.

title: Study Material Import Check
user: Calm, non-gamified learners who want to bring their own small CSV/text study materials into practice without opaque errors or a content-platform lock-in.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An independent learning-app maker asks whether a deliberately calm, non-gamified, non-subscription experience can work; the thread contains 123 comments.
Anki user reports that an empty CSV import surfaces an irrelevant 500 error with no discoverable close action, illustrating fragile learner-owned material import.

recurrence: A 123-comment discussion about calm learning and a concrete import failure point to an under-served on-ramp for people avoiding content platforms.
current_workaround: Hand-edit CSVs, search forum posts after an error, or accept a proprietary course/app's import format.
incumbents_and_gap: Anki can import many formats but is technical at the error boundary; Duolingo-like apps offer polished flows but do not accept a learner's own practice corpus.
smallest_useful_product: A static-web CSV/TSV/text inspector that previews rows, identifies blank/duplicate/broken-media fields, maps columns into a portable practice-pack manifest, and exports an import-ready file. Non-goals: hosted decks, gamification, or proprietary course content.
success_measure: At least 80% of first-time users turn a malformed sample into a valid portable pack in under five minutes without documentation.
monetization: free — an open format and frictionless first use are necessary to earn trust; paid desktop batch support could follow.
constraints: All parsing in-browser; no upload; sanitize CSV formulas and media URLs; publish a documented portable manifest.
why_distinct: It makes learner-owned materials portable and intelligible instead of becoming another engagement-oriented study destination.

title: Code Prediction Lab
user: Self-learners using an LLM while learning a programming language who need to form and test a prediction before reading an explanation or copying code.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A learner asks how people use LLMs to learn C or new programming concepts: project explanations, small code experiments, and why one approach is chosen over another.
The proposed JupyterLab extension notes that saved notebook outputs lack a record of the environment that actually produced them, so later results can look trustworthy while being irreproducible.

recurrence: Two 2026 requests identify complementary problems: learning through experiments and being able to trust/recreate the experiment later.
current_workaround: Ask a chatbot to explain code, keep ad-hoc snippets, or rerun an old notebook with unknown dependencies.
incumbents_and_gap: Jupyter and online sandboxes execute code; chat tutors explain it. Neither makes prediction-before-run, observed result, explanation, and runnable environment receipt a small learning artifact.
smallest_useful_product: Local web app that presents tiny language-specific experiments, requires a predicted output/explanation, runs a sandboxed snippet, and saves a Markdown receipt with dependency/runtime metadata. Non-goals: code generation, a hosted IDE, or a curriculum marketplace.
success_measure: In a 20-exercise pilot, learners make a prediction before execution on 75%+ of attempts and can rerun 90%+ of saved experiments unchanged one month later.
monetization: freemium — free local exercises establish utility; managed isolated runtimes for classroom groups can fund it.
constraints: Run untrusted code in strict isolated containers with resource caps; retain no learner code by default; pin and disclose runtimes.
why_distinct: The learning mechanism is committing to a falsifiable prediction, not an LLM supplying an answer.

title: Accessible Explanation Check-in
user: Teachers assigning work in AI-pervasive classes who need an inclusive, low-stakes way for each student to explain their reasoning rather than a cheating detector.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker proposes fingerprinting approved AI use for homework instead of trying to detect cheating, a direct signal that assignment provenance is unresolved.
An accessibility researcher documents that an unlabeled control leaves TalkBack users unable to understand AnkiDroid's main action, grounding the need for assistive-tech-first learning interactions.

recurrence: A 2025 assessment-provenance proposal and a 2026 accessibility report show that both proof of learning and access to the proof mechanism matter.
current_workaround: Use AI detectors, add oral exams manually, require screenshots, or accept unspecific LMS submission timestamps.
incumbents_and_gap: Turnitin-style detection tools estimate authorship and LMS quizzes score answers; neither gives teachers a short, accessible reasoning check-in with a clear student-controlled record.
smallest_useful_product: A keyboard/screen-reader-first web form for one prompt, one optional voice/text explanation, one confidence rating, and teacher review tags; export a minimal CSV/PDF receipt. Non-goals: AI detection, proctoring, biometric identity, or automatic grading.
success_measure: In a class pilot, 90% of students complete a check-in without assistance and teachers report that 70%+ of submissions provide usable evidence for follow-up.
monetization: freemium — a free small-class tier lowers adoption friction; paid school administration and retention controls fund operations.
constraints: FERPA/GDPR-aware data minimization; delete voice files on a configurable schedule; WCAG 2.2 AA; no biometric or automated misconduct inference.
why_distinct: It replaces unverifiable AI-detection claims with a humane evidence-of-reasoning ritual that is accessible by design.

title: Rubric Feedback Bundles
user: Writing teachers with many short submissions who need to preserve meaningful, human feedback while avoiding repetitive retyping.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The thread explicitly asks how teachers handle writing feedback at scale; a university teacher responds that they keep it fully manual because feedback should be worth reading.
A classroom-platform issue reports that free-text poll responses are severely truncated in recordings, showing how easily learners' own words are lost in the feedback record.

recurrence: Two teacher-facing 2026 threads identify scale pressure without accepting degraded or opaque student communication.
current_workaround: Copy/paste boilerplate comments, mark only a sample, use generic AI feedback, or leave feedback in separate documents.
incumbents_and_gap: Google Classroom, Canvas, and Grammarly can collect/annotate work, but do not optimize a teacher-owned library of editable rubric fragments with a per-student feedback receipt.
smallest_useful_product: Local-first browser tool to select reusable feedback fragments, tailor them per criterion, attach one short personal note, and export a readable student feedback page plus anonymized class misconception summary. Non-goals: essay generation, plagiarism scoring, or automated marks.
success_measure: A teacher completes feedback for 25 short pieces 30% faster while every student receives at least one specific personalized note.
monetization: one-time — individual teachers need a private dependable tool, not a per-student surveillance subscription.
constraints: Store student work locally unless the teacher explicitly exports; support accessible feedback pages; do not send submissions to an LLM.
why_distinct: It accelerates human judgment and preserves full student language rather than generating generic feedback at scale.

title: Claim Source Trail
user: Undergraduate researchers who need to learn a repeatable digital workflow from question to claim to exact supporting source passage.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An instructor asks for open, accessible tools and teaching approaches for digital research workflows with undergraduate philosophy students.
Zotero's requested reader reference popup lets readers inspect an in-text citation, see an abstract, and add or open the source, validating demand to keep source context near reading.

recurrence: An educator's 2026 workflow request and a research-tool feature thread show the persistent handoff problem between reading citations and constructing accountable claims.
current_workaround: Keep a separate notes document, copy quotations without durable locations, or assemble citations only at the end.
incumbents_and_gap: Zotero manages sources and Obsidian manages notes, but neither treats a claim, its exact quote/location, interpretation, and counterevidence check as a compact reviewable unit for novices.
smallest_useful_product: Static-web claim map: create a claim, attach source metadata plus quote/page/URL locator, tag support or challenge, and export a citation-aware outline. Non-goals: web scraping, full reference management, AI summaries, or writing the paper.
success_measure: In a workshop, 80% of students can reconstruct the evidence for each thesis paragraph from their exported trail without reopening a general notes file.
monetization: free — open teaching adoption and portable exports are core; institutions could fund hosted class templates later.
constraints: No copyrighted PDFs uploaded or redistributed; keep citations/quotes local; support CSL-JSON/BibTeX export; clearly distinguish quotation from student interpretation.
why_distinct: It teaches evidence provenance as an inspectable thinking structure, rather than becoming another citation manager or AI research wrapper.

title: Transcript Study Slicer
user: Text-first learners, including people who struggle to learn from video, who need to turn a legally available transcript into small navigable study passages.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker says they absorb text much better than video/audio and seeks an easier way to obtain and read TED/YouTube transcripts without broken copy-paste.
A learner asks for multi-file Markdown-to-Anki sync, evidence that study material often lives as many local text documents rather than a single app deck.

recurrence: A direct accessibility/format-preference request and a Markdown study-workflow request show repeated demand to make local text reusable for practice.
current_workaround: Copy malformed transcripts into notes, watch video at low speed, or manually cut text into cards one document at a time.
incumbents_and_gap: Video hosts display transcripts and Anki imports cards, but neither offers a local, transcript-first passage slicer that preserves source/time links and exports a clean learner-owned study pack.
smallest_useful_product: Browser extension that operates only on an open page's official transcript/captions or pasted text, removes line-wrap noise, lets the learner mark passages, and exports Markdown/CSV with source links. Non-goals: downloading video, bypassing access controls, transcription hosting, or automatic quiz generation.
success_measure: At least 75% of pilot users create and revisit five or more marked passages from a one-hour lecture within a week.
monetization: one-time — the value is a private accessibility utility and should not require uploading viewing history.
constraints: Respect platform terms and only process user-accessible transcript text; no audio/video redistribution; keep all data local; keyboard and screen-reader support required.
why_distinct: It improves reading access and learner-directed segmentation without relying on copyrighted content ingestion or an LLM summary layer.

title: Skill Decision Drills
user: Coaches and self-learners in procedural skills who need to rehearse decisions from real scenarios, not memorize isolated facts.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A programmer and climber describes a safety course whose classroom lecture was hard to understand, then asks whether games/cards could help learn new skills.
The 78-reaction Lichess feature request describes an opening trainer that varies opponent lines, accepts a learner's move, handles transpositions, and gives hints.

recurrence: A concrete training-transfer complaint plus a 78-reaction request for branching deliberate practice demonstrate demand beyond linear flashcards.
current_workaround: Rewatch lectures, memorize rules on cards, use instructor-led role-play, or build one-off scenario slides.
incumbents_and_gap: Kahoot and generic quiz builders favor single-answer recall; chess opening trainers are domain-specific. Small instructors lack a reusable branching decision-drill format for their own safety, field, or process scenarios.
smallest_useful_product: Offline scenario editor/player: author a decision tree with photo/text prompts, consequences, hint path, and debrief; replay with randomized branches and export aggregate misconception counts. Non-goals: regulated safety certification, scoring real-world competence, or a content marketplace.
success_measure: A coach authors one 10-node drill in under 30 minutes and learners improve correct first decisions by 25% between first and third attempt.
monetization: one-time — small coaches can buy a private authoring tool without a per-learner platform fee.
constraints: Prominent disclaimer that drills do not replace qualified instruction; no hazardous procedure advice in bundled content; local data by default.
why_distinct: It generalizes the useful branching-repertoire mechanic to learner-authored decisions rather than cloning a quiz app or chess trainer.

title: Parameter Playground
user: Teachers and self-learners explaining algorithms or mathematical models who need an honest interactive visual that changes with parameters and exposes failed intuitions.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker says TSP theory is available but asks for an interactive way to see how routes emerge as graph structure and connectivity change.
The JupyterLab proposal explains that visual notebook outputs exclude the underlying structured values needed for screen readers, sonification, or meaningful post-hoc explanation.

recurrence: Two 2026 requests show the same teaching gap: explanatory visuals need both live manipulability and non-visual access to the data behind them.
current_workaround: Use a static animation, a notebook with hidden code, or a whiteboard explanation that cannot be replayed by the learner.
incumbents_and_gap: Desmos, GeoGebra, Observable, and Jupyter are powerful general environments, but a teacher has to build accessibility narration, challenge prompts, and reproducible parameter presets themselves.
smallest_useful_product: Static-web builder for a small library of parameterized simulations: slider/table inputs, deterministic seed, accessible data table and narration fields, prediction prompt, and shareable preset URL. Non-goals: a CAS, arbitrary code execution, or generative explanations.
success_measure: A teacher publishes a reusable simulation in under one hour, and 80% of learners can state one changed parameter and its observed effect after a session.
monetization: free — open, shareable simulations are more useful when students can access them without accounts; paid private class libraries are optional later.
constraints: Use vetted deterministic model templates; show assumptions and numeric limits; require text alternatives for every visual; no unbounded user code.
why_distinct: It packages the pedagogical loop—predict, vary, inspect, explain—with accessibility, not just a charting canvas.

title: Math Circle Board
user: A volunteer running a small enrichment math circle who needs to sequence open-ended problems, see partial attempts, and preserve a lightweight learning record for a handful of students.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker wants to start a six-to-eight-child math circle centered on olympiad-style exploration rather than exam prep and asks how to make it viable.
A school using Lichess Classes extensively reports lost access to prior classes and managed student accounts, demonstrating the operational fragility of small learning-group records.

recurrence: A direct 2026 request to organize a tiny exploratory group and a school account-access report both point to lightweight cohort continuity as a real operational need.
current_workaround: Email PDFs, shared documents, group chat, and a spreadsheet that cannot represent partial strategies or lesson flow.
incumbents_and_gap: Google Classroom and Moodle are broad assignment systems; AoPS hosts communities. Neither is a deliberately small, privacy-light board for exploratory problem sessions and visible evolving attempts.
smallest_useful_product: A small-group web app with weekly problem cards, student photo/text attempt uploads, private facilitator notes, tags for strategies tried, and printable session recap. Non-goals: public child social network, adaptive test prep, video calling, or high-stakes grading.
success_measure: A facilitator runs four sessions with 6–12 learners and can produce a complete one-page recap of each learner's attempted strategies in under 10 minutes.
monetization: freemium — free tiny circles support volunteers; paid organization controls and storage fit schools or clubs.
constraints: Because minors may use it: verified adult-owned groups, minimal PII, private-by-default uploads, deletion/export controls, and no advertising or behavioral profiles.
why_distinct: It records exploratory mathematical thinking and group continuity, not marks, video meetings, or a generic LMS clone.
